Name: microbial_mediation_antagonistic_pleiotropy
Title: Transient Soil Microbiota as Mediators of Antagonistic Pleiotropy in Plant Local Adaptation
Experiment: We will build a gnotobiotic experimental system using Brassica rapa. First, we will create two defined soil microbial communities extracted from limestone and tuff field sites, each subjected to whole‑community metagenomic sequencing and selective sterilization to generate ‘home’ and ‘away’ inocula. Second, we will run a 10‑generation experimental evolution in a factorial design: Soil type (limestone/tuff) × microbial treatment (sterile, native microbiota, cross‑inoculated microbiota, and ‘pulsed’ microbiota where communities are removed via mild heat/antibiotic treatment after generation 5) × herbivory (aphids present/absent) × pollination (bumblebee/hand). At generation 10, a full reciprocal transplant experiment will measure lifetime fitness (seed set) across all previous environments. We will perform whole‑genome sequencing of each population to detect allele frequency shifts and identify SNPs exhibiting environment‑dependent pleiotropy. For candidate loci, we will use CRISPR‑Cas9 knockout lines to test fitness effects in microcosms with and without microbial partners. Metrics: relative fitness, selection coefficients, allele frequency change, and gene expression of defense‑ and growth‑related genes. Baselines: original 8‑generation experiment without microbial manipulation. Expected outcomes: (1) The presence of co‑adapted soil microbiota is required for antagonistic pleiotropy to manifest; removal after 5 generations shifts loci towards conditional neutrality. (2) Cross‑inoculation reduces local adaptation and erodes trade‑offs. Ablation studies: vary the timing of microbial removal (generations 3, 5, 7), the complexity of inocula (whole community vs. synthetic consortia of key taxa), and measure microbial recolonization dynamics.
